title: Notes of Ministry - 88 - March 1980

source.file: Various/Notes of Ministry - 88 - March 1980 (2499)/Notes of Ministry - 88 - March - Various.epub

paragraphs.text: I desire to speak about purpose of heart, about the need for being definite. We will get nowhere spiritually without resolve. The Lord Jesus is the perfect model for us. We could be well occupied with the purpose of heart that was seen in the Lord Jesus. He said, “Lo, I come … to do, O God, thy will”, Hebrews 10: 7. It was written of Him in the roll of the book, but there was a moment in time when He came into manhood to fulfil the will of God. Think of the definiteness of the purpose that marked our Lord Jesus Christ. There would have been no blessing for us, and God’s purpose would not have been secured, if it were not for the Lord Jesus coming into manhood and with purpose of heart pursuing perfectly all that the will of God involved.

So I read the verse in Luke where it says, “He stedfastly set his face to go to Jerusalem”. Think of the stedfastness of our Lord Jesus Christ. Think of His perfection in His purpose of heart, His movements never deviating to the right hand or to the left. All that He was outwardly in His movements was perfect, and all that He was inwardly in His motives and desires was perfect for the eye of God. Think of His devotion; we may well feed on the purpose of heart of our Lord Jesus Christ and on His devotion to the will of God. If we feed on this purpose of the Lord Jesus in manhood we will be built up ourselves in desire to be marked by definiteness of purpose of heart. We will get

nowhere without purpose, without decision, and what we often speak of as committal. Young people, and all of us, need this arriving at a purpose in our lives. Paul speaks of his purpose; he wrote to Timothy, “But thou hast been thoroughly acquainted with my teaching, conduct, purpose”, 2 Timothy 3: 10. Think of Paul’s purpose. How did Paul maintain his links with the Lord Jesus? How did he become the devoted servant he was? By his purpose of heart.

It is seen perfectly and absolutely in our Lord Jesus Christ. The days of His receiving up were fulfilled, but He moves toward Jerusalem with purpose of heart. There were those who rejected Him because He moved in this way, but without deviation “he stedfastly set his face to go to Jerusalem”. For Him that meant suffering, the pathway from the mount of transfiguration down to Golgotha, and to the sufferings of the cross. He was crucified, the object of ridicule, of the animosity of men, with Satan behind them, but He also was the Victim of the sufferings He underwent from the hand of God; but He stedfastly set His face.

It says in John 19: 17, “And he went out, bearing his cross”; He, “knowing all things that were coming upon him, went forth” (John 18: 4). The stedfastness, the purpose, of our Lord Jesus Christ we do well to dwell upon continually and feed upon so that we too should be marked by increased purpose of heart.

I read about these people in Acts 11. “They then who had been scattered abroad passed through the country to Phoenicia and Cyprus and Antioch, speaking the word to no one but to Jews alone. But there were certain of them, Cyprians and Cyrenians, who entering into Antioch spoke to the Greeks also, announcing the glad tidings of the Lord Jesus. And the Lord’s hand was with them, and a great number believed and turned to the Lord. And the report concerning them reached the ears of the assembly which was in Jerusalem, and they sent out Barnabas to go through as far as Antioch: who, having arrived and seeing the grace of God, rejoiced, and exhorted all with purpose of heart to abide with the Lord”.

These converts in Antioch actually became the assembly in Antioch; they became a remarkable assembly. How was it formed? The basis was Barnabas’s exhortation, he “exhorted all with purpose of heart to abide with the Lord”. He exhorted them, and then he went away to Tarsus to seek out Saul, and Barnabas and Saul taught for a whole year and assembly conditions were established in Antioch. It is one of the assemblies which was formed from among the nations. There is no fault found with it; there seemed to be normal conditions in Antioch. It was based on this purpose of heart as to which Barnabas exhorted. It says, “And so it was with them that for a whole year they were gathered together in the assembly and taught a large crowd”. There was constructive teaching in Antioch for a whole year, and there was a positive result in testimony and for the pleasure of God, and the service of God was established there.

Later we find that they were ministering to the Lord and fasting, and the Holy Spirit had His way in that local company. “The Holy Spirit said, Separate me now Barnabas and Saul”, Acts 13: 2. You can see, dear brethren, the results of answering to the exhortation with purpose of heart to abide with the Lord. We know we have deviated, but the word would come to us afresh now that purpose of heart might mark us to abide with the Lord; that the Lord may have His way with us, that we may be subject persons, obedient persons, living by the word of God, ready for instruction. It is really the good ground, the honest and good heart, of Luke 8: 15. He “exhorted all with purpose of heart to abide with the Lord”. That exhortation would come afresh, I believe, to oneself and to each one of us here, to abide with the Lord, to abide in the area of the truth, to abide under His direction, to be available to Him, to take up responsibilities locally with His interests in view for the promotion of what is for His pleasure and for the pleasure and service of God. What a privilege we have! We need to come to decision, to come to committal in purpose of heart.

I have read of three persons in the Old Testament who were marked by this feature, and the first one is Daniel who was a youth. In modern language we speak of teenagers; that is what Daniel was, but one who had purpose of heart. We do not need to wait until we are old to arrive at purpose of heart, we can have it when we are young. Daniel was carried away in the first captivity as we read—“In the third year of the reign of Jehoiakim king of Judah came Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon unto Jerusalem, and besieged it. And the Lord gave Jehoiakim king of Judah into his hand, and a part of the vessels of the house of God; and he carried them into the land of Shinar”, Daniel 1: 1, 2. Daniel was among the youths who were carried away in this captivity from Jerusalem to Babylon. He was looked upon by Nebuchadnezzar as being a possibility for his system, for Babylon. He was sent to the university of those days to be trained to promote the idolatrous system of Babylon. Daniel might have conceded, just accepted the opportunity, but it says that “Daniel purposed in his heart”. He was allocated the daily provision of the king’s delicate food and the wine that he drank which, if he had partaken of it, would have fitted him for the Babylonish system; but he purposed in his heart not to pollute himself with the king’s delicate food, nor with the wine which he drank, and he requested the prince of the eunuchs that he might not have to pollute himself. There was no provision made for conscience, but he requested; he was subject and respectful. How good it would be if our young people came to a certain purpose of heart not to pollute themselves, not to fit into the system of this world. Daniel not only requested not to be polluted with the king’s delicate food and the wine that he drank, but he directed the prince of the eunuchs as to what kind of food he should be fed on; the kind of food he requested was pulse and water. The king’s delicate food was no doubt attractive to the man after the flesh. It would be well presented; it would be colourful; it would appeal to young people. Daniel in his purpose of heart rejected it and requested that he should be given pulse.

Now pulse is very unattractive to the natural man; it does not look good; no matter how you presented pulse it would not be all that attractive; but it is basic food. It was food to build up Daniel in his constitution to be separate from the Babylonish system of things, and to be here in testimony and for the glory and pleasure of God. Daniel could have been one of the prominent men socially in Babylon, but he was separate from it all. There was a secret in this; Daniel had a secret in his soul which does not comes out until chapter 6, verse 10, where we are told that Daniel had his windows open toward Jerusalem. He was in Babylon, but his windows were toward Jerusalem where God’s house was. This first captivity was not a complete captivity; there was something left in Jerusalem. It was not until a number of years afterwards that Jerusalem was destroyed by Nebuchadnezzar when Zedekiah was king; this was the first movement of captivity, so there were still vessels left in Jerusalem, and that is where Daniel’s heart was. It was the appreciation of what was positively there for God that preserved Daniel from being linked on with, and becoming part of, the world’s system.

For us it would be light in our souls as to the Lord Jesus Christ in heaven and the Holy Spirit active in an order of things down here for the pleasure of God. Because of the positive light Daniel had he requested that he would not be polluted with the king’s delicate food and the wine that he drank, but that he be fed with pulse and water. Now what would this pulse be for us today? The king’s delicate food and the wine that he drank is what builds up persons for this world’s system, but pulse and water is food for persons who are committed to the will of God. Pulse is an excellent food, even naturally, but unattractive, as I said. We have reading material the like of which is not found anywhere else. I do not mind where you go you will not find reading material such as is available to us in the day in which we are. We have the Holy Scriptures in an accurate translation; we have ministries which are reliable; I think that is like the pulse.

The Holy Scriptures may be unattractive to us when we are young. I can remember a time when I knew the Lord as my Saviour but I had little or no desire for the Scriptures. I could see my father reading his Bible, and I would see him too with books of reliable ministry, and he would be engrossed in enjoying these things, but I did not have that same purpose. I did not have any taste for the Scriptures until I began to read the Scriptures, and the more I read them the more I desired to read them. I had no desire to read ministry until I began to read the ministry; the more ministry I read the more I desired to read, not just for memorizing it, but I found food, I found what cleansed my thoughts, occupied my mind with what was good and built up the soul in the knowledge of the will of God. Such reading matter builds up manhood according to God. I think that is what answers to the pulse and water. It is simple, not attractive to man after the flesh; you have to acquire a taste for it. Daniel had this taste; he purposed in his heart. Let us all purpose in heart to have this taste. Even as believers we need our taste changed.

When the children of Israel came out of Egypt, after three days in the wilderness they came to Marah and the waters of Marah were bitter. God showed Moses wood “and he cast it into the waters and the waters became sweet”, Exodus 15: 25. In the history of the children of Israel the waters changed, but in our experience we change, our taste changes. What is bitter to the man after the flesh becomes attractive because Moses is shown wood; for us it is really the Lord Jesus Christ here in manhood in wilderness circumstances, here for the will of God. The appreciation of Him changes our taste, we find the waters can be appropriated, just as Daniel’s taste was for this pulse and water. Dear brethren, we need to arrive at this purpose of heart. The more we read of this world’s literature the less taste we will have for the Scriptures or for ministry that will help us, but the more we commit ourselves to the Scriptures and to ministry that will help us the less taste we will have for what the world offers.

I do not often go into a book shop but I was in one recently to get some books for children and I saw books for every taste. Satan is able by books to cater for every depraved desire and every taste of the human heart, no matter what it is. Of course, some of these books are instructive, and some have to be read at school, but many of them are novels, and there are books on all subjects; but there are the Scriptures and there are books that are reliable, books that will build up our souls in the appreciation of the Lord Jesus, and build up our souls in the kind of manhood that is here for the will of God. The pulse and water is like reading material which we need to commit ourselves to. You will never get a taste for the Scriptures or ministries that will help you until you begin to appropriate them, then your taste will change. May we all commit ourselves with purpose of heart to this line of Daniel. He began young. There are great opportunities for young people, I believe the Lord specially helps persons who commit themselves when they are young; you cannot begin too young on this line of Daniel. May we all have this purpose of heart.

Now David in Psalm 132 says he swore unto Jehovah, and vowed. You wonder that he was so committed, that his purpose was so definite—“How he swore unto Jehovah, vowed unto the Mighty One of Jacob—I will not come into the tent of my house, I will not go up to the couch of my bed; I will not give sleep to mine eyes, slumber to mine eyelids, until I find out a place for Jehovah, habitations for the Mighty One of Jacob ...”. You wonder that David could go so far in his purpose of heart to provide what was pleasing to God down here. He goes on to say, “Behold, we heard of it (that is the ark) at Ephratah, we found it in the fields of the wood”. Think what it was for David’s heart when he found it! He heard of it; it was in what has been described as ‘cold storage’ with Abinadab up on the hill “in the fields of the wood” (see 1 Samuel 7: 1); and he found it. The first ten verses of this psalm give us David’s purpose and exercises. From verse 13 we get God’s answer to David’s exercises. The fact is that David’s exercises coincided with God’s desires. David’s

exercises were towards Zion; Zion is called David’s city; it is a city that was acquired by David’s exercises—Jehovah says, “For Jehovah hath chosen Zion; he hath desired it for his dwelling—This is my rest for ever; here will I dwell” (Psalm 132: 13, 14). Think of David’s exercises and purpose of heart being in such a direction that Jehovah can say, This is what I am looking for, this is what I had in mind from the beginning, that a service should be established for Me. We need to be set, dear brethren, with purpose of heart for what is for God’s pleasure, and the service of God. So from verse 13 it is God’s answer to David’s prayers, to David’s swearing to Jehovah, David’s vow, the intenseness of it. What David was exercised about was exactly what God desired. Would that be the line of our exercises? Jehovah says, “This is my rest for ever; here will I dwell, for I have desired it”.

The fact is, dear brethren, that God is finding at this time in which we are, in spite of all the confusion and the breakdown, what His heart desires, coming about through the exercises of His people to provide something suited to Him. We have local exercises that conditions should be provided suited for the Lord to come to. I am not one of those who claim the Lord’s presence, that the Lord is with us; my concern is that we should keep providing conditions suitable for the Lord to come. I am not so much concerned about claiming that the Lord is with us; I am more concerned that we be with the Lord in what His mind is. He is with them who are with Him; that is a constant, daily, weekly, exercise, to be with Him, and provide conditions suited to Him. So Jehovah says, “I will abundantly bless her provision; I will satisfy her needy ones with bread; And I will clothe her priests with salvation”. David requests, “Let thy priests be clothed with righteousness” (Psalm 132: 9); God’s answer is, “I will clothe her priests with salvation”. We are to be in the enjoyment of salvation. As a brother said earlier today, there is a fulness about our salvation; there is liberty about it; it leads on to eternal life; that is the fulness of salvation available to us at the present time. David requests, “and let thy saints shout for joy”; Jehovah says, “and her saints shall shout aloud for joy”.

There is excess in the blessing that the Lord bestows on His people, but it comes about through David’s exercises, through purpose of heart. It will come about if we are exercised in this way in our localities; there will be something for the service and pleasure of God. God will say, This is what I have been looking for; this is what I have pleasure in. He may have been deprived of it in certain localities for a long time, but now He can say, Here it is for My delight. It was David’s purpose of heart that led to this, and then, you might say, the Lord takes over because He finds conditions suited—“This is my rest for ever; here will I dwell”.

Is it not worthwhile going through exercises to provide something for the divine pleasure? There is so much around us in confusion, so much that is displeasing to Him. We often speak of certain things around us as feeling them, but the Lord feels them far more than we do. We are only just beginning to learn how the Lord feels about certain things. That is negative; what we need to do is to provide what is positive for His pleasure.

We perhaps do not fully realize what it means to the Lord to have overcomers available in localities down here of whom He can approve. It means more to Him than we realize. He would say, This is what I am looking for. It is not a question of persons so gathered claiming anything; they do not need to claim; it is a question of what the Lord says. The woman who anointed the Lord’s head as recorded at the end of Matthew and the end of Mark was so attracted to the Lord, and loved Him so much, that she brought that ointment and poured it out upon His head. She would say, ‘I just did what I felt like doing’; she would not think there was anything great about it. Oh how the Lord appreciated what she did! The Lord said, “What she could she has done”, Mark 14: 8. He said that wheresoever the gospel is preached what she did shall be spoken of. She never expected such approbation.

I sometimes think that the saints in the assembly in Philadelphia, when they got that letter by the hand of John, would say to themselves, ‘We did not expect such approval; we are only a feeble few here; there is more gift in Laodicea’. We would be greatly encouraged if we could see things as the Lord sees them, and feel things as the Lord feels them. Some overcomers in a locality gathering together for the Lord’s supper means more to Him than we realize; it does indeed. If we only saw it through His eyes we would be greatly encouraged and built up in His service. He would say, as it were, “This is my rest for ever; here will I dwell”. It is His own pronouncement, His own approval and approbation.

Now just a word about Ezra, who was in a day of recovery such as we are in. What impressed me was that Ezra “directed his heart to seek the law of Jehovah and to do it, and to teach in Israel the statutes and the ordinances”. He directed his heart; he set himself in this direction; and this, dear brethren, is needed. You might say he directed his heart toward the understanding of divine principles; they are needed in the day in which we are. We need to direct our hearts in this; there needs to be care, leadership, and overseership; all these features are needed in our localities; there will always be need for care. The more numbers there are, the more these things are needed. We need a lead in the right direction, and care, and maintenance of divine principles. We need to direct our hearts, like Ezra, if there are to be conditions pleasing to the Lord.

May we be encouraged to have the purpose of heart of Daniel, and all of us be committed with purpose of heart in spiritual resolve to provide what is pleasing to the Lord, and then let us have regard to divine principles, the maintenance of what is suited to Him in our localities, helping others into it also. May the Lord help us in these things.

I desire to speak of the Lord’s relations with us, particularly having restoration in view; and then of our relations with Him. In the first scripture, the Lord came into the circumstances of two of His own and, in the second, two of His own came into His circumstances, involving the truth on the one hand as to piety and, on the other, as to spirituality. We should be marked by both features and particularly the latter, because we shall soon be in spiritual conditions for ever. Meanwhile, we are in provisional conditions, such as are envisaged in Luke 24, in which the Lord has to do with us. He came in to serve these two persons so that they might be delivered from their own circumstances in order to be found in the circle where He is supreme. To Laodicea He says, “If any one hear my voice and open the door, I will come in unto him and sup with him”—as we see in Luke 24 and then He adds, “and he with me”—as in John 1, and that leads into eternity. The great need at this present juncture is to be led into eternity. John wrote in order that we might acquire and cultivate the taste for what is spiritual, and the Lord serves us now with this end in view.

Now these brethren were on the way to their objective, Emmaus, and they were downcast. Is any one here downcast? If so, you too are the object of the Lord’s interest. You might hope that He will send someone to help you, but He sent no one to help these two. He undertook to serve them directly and personally Himself, with no intermediary, and they were amenable to His service. The psalmist enquires, “Why art thou cast down, my soul?”, Psalm 42: 11. If this is so, look away from yourself and your circumstances to God revealed in Christ, and you will find that He will be to you “a help in distresses, very readily found”, Psalm 46: 1. The Lord is traversing all the distance required in love to serve His own, for He values every one redeemed by His blood. There is a beautiful word of appeal in Jeremiah 14: 7–9, “Jehovah, though our iniquities testify against us, do thou act for thy name’s sake; for our backslidings are many—we have sinned against thee. Thou hope of Israel, its Saviour in the time of trouble ...”—that is what Jesus was to these two; it is like Paul’s reference to “Christ Jesus our hope”, 1 Timothy 1: l—“why wilt thou be as a stranger in the land, and as a traveller that turneth aside to stay a night?” Think of His being prepared as a wayfaring man, so to speak, to turn aside to stay a night with you. He would turn aside if you let Him. He is standing at the door and is knocking. Just open it to Him.

As going towards Emmaus they were in a dangerous position, but the Lord saved them from it. Had they not been amenable to His service they would not have returned to Jerusalem and to the company into the midst of which He came. So He journeyed with them and listened to all that they had to say as they confided in Him. You can confide in Him too, even if you cannot confide in the nearest and dearest to you naturally. We all need to confide more in Him.

So they drew near to their own village and home, and as the Lord spoke to them their heart burned within them—for they were not lukewarm Laodiceans—and they began to consider for Him. Are we considering for Him? So far as this dispensation is concerned, the day is declining. Are we concerned that the Lord should stay with us when the day is declining?

Alas, I see signs that some are declining. Hosea speaks of Ephraim having “gray hairs ... here and there upon him, and he knoweth it not”, Hosea 7: 9. Gray hairs suggest spiritual decline. Decline is sad enough, but to be in that state and not know it is worse, for that is the condition in Laodicea. Thou “knowest not that thou art the wretched and the miserable, and poor, and blind, and naked”; but these were not such. They were considering for Him, and He entered in and stayed with them. Jeremiah continues, “Yet thou, Jehovah, art in the midst of us, and we are called by thy name—leave us not”. Do you ever consider the possibility that the Lord might leave us? There must be suitable conditions if He is to stay. Lydia recognised the need to be judged faithful by Paul if he was to abide with her. So we have to attend to matters if He is to stay with us. He allows moral exercises to come in which test our faithfulness, and as we are faithful He will not leave us. Are we sufficiently concerned that conditions should be such that He might remain with us?

We might be satisfied with the Lord being with us, but He has more in view. He cannot be held in provisional conditions. He disappeared from them, and that occasioned fresh exercise with them to return to Jerusalem the same hour. It does not seem to have taken them long to get back either, for God was working with them that they might reach the objective in His mind, which was that they should be found in the company into which the Lord came. He has the same objective today. Numbers may be few, but consider what is there potentially for Him. In the broken company in Luke they were not bemoaning disappointed hopes but rather were they in a state of spiritual jubilation—“The Lord is indeed risen and has appeared to Simon” (Luke 24: 34). They were doubtless thrilled as He Himself came and stood in their midst. He would just serve us to the great end that we too might experience the thrill of heart and stimulation to our affections as He presents Himself living.

Now in the second scripture we have two disciples who were the product of John the baptist’s ministry. There is a great need of persons like them, born and bred in the soil of a ministry which reaches into the depths of the conscience and soul. John patronised nobody; perhaps some might have felt insulted by his ministry and would have turned away. But John was an effective minister because he had come to it that “He must increase, but I must decrease” (John 3: 30); not just disappearing a little, but right out of sight. It is a man who is nothing who can lead to Christ. I may know that I am nothing, but the test is whether I am nothing (see J. N. Darby’s ‘Letters’, Vol. 2, p.473).

So John pointed to Jesus as the Lamb of God and, hearing him speaking, they followed Him. Are you really a follower of Jesus, or has someone, maybe without your realising it, come between your soul and Christ? In these times of recurring sorrow and pressure salvation lies in following Him. As we follow we become objects of His interest. “What seek ye?”, He said. They wished to know where He dwelt. Their desire went beyond having the Lord in their circumstances; they wanted to come into His. He did not give them the address, but said, “Come and see”, and they did. “They abode with him that day”.

Have you come and seen where He abides? If through deep exercise you have, you will never go elsewhere. Many prospect around as to which company of believers is right, this or that, and choose to be identified with it, but it is not exactly a question of a company in this passage. It is a Person who holds them—‘Where abidest thou? ... They ... saw where He abode; and they abode with Him that day’. Then it says, “It was about the tenth hour”. I wish we had a deeper sense of how time is rolling on and of the near return of the Lord. “He that comes will come, and will not delay”, Hebrews 10: 37. At the tenth hour there is not much time left before night descends on this world. The night is coming when no one can work; but these two disciples were with the Lord in His circumstances in the little time left that day.

Now in Chronicles we have certain who “dwelt with the king for his work”. I would appeal to every brother and sister in regard to this. You may feel that you have no particular service, so you leave the work to others. One result of God’s work in us by the Spirit is that there is a desire to be serviceable to the Lord. If you are one of His followers, you are potentially one who can serve Him. He said, “If any one serve me, let him follow me; and where I am, there also shall be my servant”, John 12: 26. Being with the Lord relates to the present—not only to the future—and to the present enjoyment of communion with Him. Some want what is new and regard all else as old fashioned, but in this scripture it says, “And these are ancient things”. We are to go on with these ancient things, with what was at the beginning of the dispensation, as those who abide “among plantations and enclosures: there they dwelt with the king for his work”.

These are persons who care for the local assembly so that there may be conditions there exclusively for Christ. Your local plantation cannot be left to look after itself, it must be cultivated or else the weeds will grow quickly enough as in the field of the sluggard (Proverbs 24: 30–34). It is not great exploits that are required, but being with the Lord, in communion with Him, in relation to His work. Let us be found as “God’s fellow-workmen”—journeymen, fellows doing the chief’s work (see note to 1 Corinthians 3: 9).

Let us not despise the day of small things, but rather be amenable to the service of Christ to gather what is in His mind, to be deepened in the desire to find where He dwells and to dwell with Him in relation to His work, for His name’s sake.

I wanted to continue a little as to what we have had before us as to what is heavenly, because I think what is heavenly is the test at the present day. I suppose it is the same in this country as elsewhere that the truth of what is heavenly has largely been given up. The work of Christ has not been given up, but the truth of what is heavenly has been given up. So I have read these scriptures to draw attention to certain features of what is heavenly. The heavenly side of the truth brings in what suits Christ. I think we can see that what suits ourselves will have an end. Mr. Stoney said that what suits man will end in Babylon, and as to what suits Christ, the consummation of it is in the new Jerusalem (N.S. Vol.3 pp.175, 181).

It is a very fine thing, dear brethren, to be among those who are suitable to Christ and who are occupied in that which suits Christ and I think that what is heavenly is presented to us constantly as an opportunity. It is presented to us as an opportunity because it is not something which we can have experience of casually. The devil is constantly set against the saints taking on what is heavenly. I think in the first scripture we get set before us heavenly territory; it is the opportunity for taking it up, and the devil is set against that. In the second scripture we have some suggestion of heavenly company; David speaks about “with me”. In the final scripture we could perhaps see that there is the possibility of pursuing heavenly ministry.

We know the history in Genesis. There had been failure on the part of Abram, and there has been failure on the part of all of us, which the enemy would use to hinder us. Abram had gone down to Egypt and he had, typically, got to the point of disowning the assembly there.

Let us avoid any situation where we may do that—he said that Sarah was his sister. We could say that, you see; that would be acceptable in the world around, the religious world. We may have a link with Christ, which is respectable, but she was his wife, and that involves a deeper bond, it involves being to another.

Abram had come out of Egypt, and had judged Egypt in his heart, but he had led Lot into Egypt, and the world was still there in Lot’s heart. How solemn, dear brethren, that we have had a part in leading into what is worldly, and have not been able to recover all our brethren from it. Peter speaks later of Lot’s righteous soul, and yet they could not dwell together any more. There is a point where there is a separation between them. I would specially appeal to those who are younger today, for what was set before Lot was as the garden of Jehovah in his eyes. How deluded we can be, beloved! It was as the garden of Jehovah; it was very attractive to him. At the present time there is what is attractive to us, especially when we are younger, in the world around. But the key to it is that Lot chose for himself. He chose for himself all the plain of the Jordan. Beloved younger brethren, let us search our hearts as to whether we are choosing for ourselves today, or whether we are choosing what suits Christ.

So Jehovah says to Abram, “Lift up now thine eyes”. It is a good thing to lift up our eyes. We are most of us creatures of circumstances; we are influenced by the day we are in and by our circumstances. I think our brother has been encouraging us today to lift up our eyes and look. God has divine territory to show to us. I suppose in our experience what we have taken up of heavenly territory has been very small; I suppose those who are older would admit that. We may have some few impressions; would that we had more of these experiences so that our eyes would sweep over divine territory, heavenly territory! We are tested in the service of God as to our scope in relation to what is heavenly. And yet God says, “Look ... northward and southward and eastward and westward; for all the land that thou seest will I give to thee”. Dear brethren, let us begin to look at heavenly territory.

So you find that Abram settles here. I read this scripture because of the reference to Mamre, which refers to stability. Our brother has spoken of what is stable. It has been said searchingly that stability of soul is very rare. I would like us all to think of that—stability of soul. But Abram dwelt by the oaks of Mamre, and he built an altar there. I do not want to speak much more about this scripture, but I think it is important to see that he was in a stable position and people knew that he was there. In the next chapter, after the conflict, they “went and told Abram the Hebrew, and he dwelt by the oaks of Mamre” (Genesis 14: 13). Can you be guaranteed to be there, beloved? If there is a crisis in a place, will all the young people know that you will be there? Will the older ones know that, whatever may occur in the testimony, you will be found there in a stable position? Let us be known as stable persons. Let our position be known, that we are dwelling there, and let others have the confidence that we shall be there, if it please Him, until He comes.

In 2 Samuel 19 you get the opportunity presented of spiritual company, heavenly company. Barzillai, it says, was a very great man, one who had maintained the king. He was one who had to some extent hazarded his life in relation to the king, he had put himself into danger to maintain David. But now the crisis was over. We sometimes shine better in a crisis; we seem to learn more of God in adversity. But now the crisis was over and you get this lovely invitation—“Pass thou over with me, and I will maintain thee with me in Jerusalem”. Dear brethren, what a prospect! We come to occasions like this and we touch something of the sweetness of being with Christ and maintained by Him. And yet Barzillai was not ready, you may say, for heavenly company. Are you like that? If there is a crisis in a place you can help the saints, but in the opening up and development of what is heavenly you would rather be in ‘your own place’ (verse 39). There was one young man who was ready to go, Chimham, whose name means ‘longing’. How fine it is, even if there are those who have stood aside from going in for what is heavenly, that there are those who have gone on. We can see those here today who have gone on despite the difficulties, despite the breakdown and wreckage which have come in, those who still have a longing for the company of Christ. Let us be preserved in it, beloved, to enjoy seeing the saints and enjoy the company of Christ amongst them. It has been said that the over-Jordan epistles—that is those which take up what is heavenly—involve what is collective. How thankful we are for one another! Barzillai speaks about what he cannot discern—“Can thy servant taste what I eat and what I drink?” Do we feel like that, dear brethren? Have we a taste for spiritual things? Do we have an appetite for them? Can I taste what I eat and drink? Is there satisfaction? How much satisfaction there is to listen to a heavenly ministry! Can I hear any more the voice of singing men and singing women? May the sweetness of links among the saints never fail with any one of us. He says—‘I will go a little way’. There is a need, not for those who go a little way, but for those of whom we are reminded who “gave themselves first to the Lord, and to us by God’s will”, 2 Corinthians 8: 5.

In Acts 15 we have Paul and Barnabas, and here you get the parting of the ways with them. Barnabas was another great man. How many of the saints we know and love and who have served the Lord and His people in the past have stepped aside for the moment and are out of the path of what is heavenly. Think of what Barnabas had done! He was one who had hazarded his life for the saints. He had laid his possessions at the feet of the apostles. He had had to do with the establishment of the truth at Jerusalem and had laboured with Paul at Antioch in relation to the local assembly. And yet there comes a point where he leaves Paul.

Let us be searched, beloved, for what diverted Barnabas was what was natural. Let us never fail to see that what is heavenly is not what is natural. The natural will hinder and if it has too much hold of us it will divert us from heavenly ministry.

You get in each of these instances a man who comes forward. If Lot fails, Abram comes forward; if Barzillai steps aside, then Chimham comes forward; and if Barnabas steps aside, then Silas comes forward. Thank God for those who have come forward in our day, and for the fact that Paul “went forth, committed by the brethren to the grace of God ... confirming the assemblies”. The assemblies will be confirmed as what is heavenly is maintained. If any of us give up what is heavenly then the enemy will have done his work. But what is for Christ’s heart today should be prime with every one of us until that day when we shall be with Him for ever. Our beloved sister in this place is now with Christ. Soon we shall all be with Him and the time of testing and pressure will be over. Yet the present day offers a unique opportunity for taking up and holding what is heavenly, the knowledge and experience of Christ where He is. May we be encouraged, for His name’s sake.

You could never have the bow if you had not the cloud. God brings the cloud—you may have tribulation; it is the normal surrounding of the saint; but when God brings a cloud, an exercise, a difficulty, look out for the bow. There is not a sorrow or an exercise or a difficulty, but God means you to have through it the light of the beauty and blessedness of Christ in a way you never had before. So that you may have a peculiar sense of God’s faithfulness, and that nothing can separate you from the love of Christ nor from the love of God; that is the bow.
paragraphs.source: C. A. Coates (‘Outline of Genesis’, p.82)

paragraphs.text: This keeping the flesh mortified is the great thing, the secret of all strength, in practical difficulties; and nothing will do it but living in communion and fellowship with the Lord.
paragraphs.source: J. N. Darby (‘Collected Wrtgs’, N.S. Vol. 17, p.359)
